reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: A benign, inherited disorder producing chronic or fluctuating conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal liver tests
Patients are usually asymptomatic or have only mild jaundice, and life expectancy is normal so no specific treatment is needed
It is caused by an autosomal recessive defect in the canalicular transporter MRP2 (encoded by ABCC2) that exports conjugated bilirubin into bile
The liver is grossly black due to accumulation of a dark, melanin-like pigment in hepatocytes, a striking but harmless histological feature
Total serum bilirubin is usually only modestly raised and jaundice may be intensified by pregnancy, oral contraceptives, or intercurrent illness
Total urinary coproporphyrin is normal but the proportion of the isomer coproporphyrin I is markedly increased, a pattern that helps distinguish it from Rotor syndrome
Unlike hepatic obstruction, there is no pruritus and alkaline phosphatase and bile acids are normal
The main clinical importance is recognising it as benign to avoid unnecessary investigation for cholestatic or hepatocellular disease
reference.pathophysiology: Dubin-Johnson syndrome results from an autosomal recessive deficiency of the multidrug resistance-associated protein 2 (MRP2/ABCC2), the ATP-dependent transporter on the canalicular membrane that secretes conjugated bilirubin and other organic anions into bile. Because bilirubin is conjugated normally within the hepatocyte but cannot be exported efficiently, conjugated bilirubin refluxes into the circulation, giving a predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with bilirubinuria. Impaired transport also alters coproporphyrin handling, shifting the urinary isomer ratio toward coproporphyrin I. A distinctive dark pigment, thought to derive from metabolites of adrenaline, accumulates in lysosomes and blackens the liver but causes no functional impairment. The disorder is entirely benign and does not progress to fibrosis or cirrhosis.
additionalInvestigations: Fractionated serum bilirubin confirming a conjugated predominance
Urinary coproporphyrin analysis showing a raised proportion of the coproporphyrin I isomer with normal total excretion
Liver function tests confirming normal aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, and bile acids
Imaging to exclude biliary obstruction where clinically warranted
Genetic testing for ABCC2 mutations when confirmation is desired
Liver biopsy only if needed, showing characteristic black pigment
redFlags: Features that would be atypical for a benign disorder, such as pruritus, raised alkaline phosphatase, or abnormal aminotransferases, prompting search for another cause
New or worsening jaundice with systemic illness suggesting superimposed hepatobiliary disease
Deepening jaundice unexplained by pregnancy, hormonal therapy, or intercurrent illness
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign with a normal life expectancy; jaundice may fluctuate and deepen with pregnancy, hormonal contraceptives, or intercurrent illness but requires no specific treatment.
pitfalls: Subjecting patients to extensive or invasive workup for a harmless disorder
Confusing it with obstructive or hepatocellular jaundice
Failing to use the urinary coproporphyrin isomer pattern to distinguish it from Rotor syndrome
Attributing every rise in bilirubin to the syndrome without excluding a superimposed second pathology
